nameStory: The name 'hawkweed' comes from an ancient belief that hawks would eat these plants to sharpen their eyesight for hunting. This particular species gets its 'New England' name from being one of the most common hawkweeds found in our region, even though it's actually a European immigrant that made itself at home here.
description: New England hawkweed is a medium-sized perennial wildflower that produces cheerful yellow daisy-like blooms from summer into fall. This European native has naturalized throughout New England, growing 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems. Like other members of the sunflower family, what looks like a single flower is actually a cluster of tiny individual flowers packed together into a flower head.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flower heads about 1 inch across with numerous thin, narrow petals (actually ray flowers) that feel papery to the touch. Multiple flower heads cluster at the top of branching stems, creating a loose, airy display.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves with prominent veins and slightly toothed edges that feel somewhat rough and hairy when rubbed between your fingers. Leaves get smaller as they go up the stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms clumps 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems that create an open, somewhat sprawling appearance. The plant has a weedy, informal look rather than a neat garden appearance.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces fluffy white seed heads similar to dandelions but smaller. Each seed has a parachute-like tuft of white bristles that catches the wind for dispersal.

habitat: Look for New England hawkweed in disturbed soils, roadsides, old fields, and woodland edges throughout New England. It thrives in areas with some human disturbance and can tolerate both sunny and partially shaded locations with average to poor soil conditions.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the base, forming a rosette of lance-shaped foliage. Stems begin to elongate as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flower heads opening in succession from July through August. Plants reach their full height during this time.
seasonality.fall: Late flowers may continue blooming into early fall, followed by the characteristic fluffy white seed heads that disperse in autumn breezes.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back, but the root system remains alive underground, ready to sprout new growth in spring.

funFact: Despite being called 'New England' hawkweed, this plant is actually a European colonist that arrived sometime after human settlement and liked our region so much it decided to stay permanently!
confusionNotes: New England hawkweed can be tricky to distinguish from other hawkweeds without close examination. The branching flower clusters and medium height help separate it from the low-growing mouse-ear hawkweed or the single-stemmed Canada hawkweed. When in doubt, remember that hawkweeds as a group all have that distinctive yellow daisy-flower and dandelion-like seeds.
contextualKnowledge: This species is considered a noxious weed in some western states where it can crowd out native plants, but in New England it's been part of the naturalized flora for so long that it's generally accepted as part of our weedy plant community.
compareHints: Among New England's hawkweeds, this species stands out for its multi-branched flowering stems and medium height. Canada hawkweed tends to be taller with flowers clustered at the top of mostly unbranched stems, while mouse-ear hawkweed stays much lower to the ground. The branching pattern and overall 'bushy' appearance are your best clues for identifying this particular hawkweed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Panicled hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by being much taller and more upright than species like rattlesnakeweed or spotted hawkweed.
Among its hawkweed relatives, rattlesnakeweed stands out for its ground-hugging rosette growth pattern and prominent leaf veining.
Rough hawkweed is much more bristly and hairy than its relatives like panicled hawkweed or Canada hawkweed, which have smoother stems and leaves.
Among the many hawkweed species in New England, common hawkweed is distinguished by its branching growth habit and grayish, hairy leaves.
Among New England hawkweeds, Canada hawkweed stands out for its exceptionally narrow, smooth leaves and tall, elegant stature.
Among New England's hawkweeds, spotted hawkweed stands out for its tall, branching flower stems and tendency to grow in disturbed soils.
Among New England's hawkweeds, wall hawkweed is distinguished by its preference for rocky, vertical surfaces and its distinctly heart-shaped leaves with purple veining.
Among New England's hawkweeds, Beaked Hawkweed stands out for its extremely small flowers and very hairy lower stem.
Among its hawkweed relatives, Robinson's hawkweed stays much smaller than New England hawkweed or Canada hawkweed, which can grow much taller.
